source.title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Lorenz Hufe; Jim Berend; Thomas Wiegand; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses neuron polysemanticity as motivation and studies SAE components in CLIP, but it does not measure whether individual neurons respond to multiple unrelated inputs or test any listed version.
record.gate_note: The study analyzes semantic alignment and prediction relevance of SAE components, not the mixed responses of individual neurons described by the claim. Its CLIP text-image failure cases concern prompt ambiguity, typographic artifacts, and spurious correlations; these do not establish neuron polysemanticity. Cited claims about monosemantic features and sparse feature hypotheses are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study cites neuron polysemanticity (Toy Models of Superposition) only as motivation for using SAEs on CLIP's final class-token embeddings. It then measures SAE-component clarity, concept diversity, attribution faithfulness and failure modes. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, and it does not test causes, architecture effects or measurement dependence. The neural-basis comparison in Fig. 4b counts unique concept labels per basis, which is not a polysemanticity rate.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that combining SAEs with attribution patching exposes reliance on unexpected or spurious components in CLIP: polysemous prompts, compound nouns, typography and spurious correlations. They draw no conclusion about neuron polysemanticity, noting only that it may remain a challenge for SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders and attribution patching on CLIP embeddings rather than the neuron-level methods or activation-function comparisons associated with the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: For text-image failure cases, prompt enrichment improves robustness particularly for typographic distractors, while gains vary by failure type; templating helps typography modestly but is less effective for polysemy. Attribution results also depend on the choice of reference samples.

fits_no_version.finding: Most SAE components in CLIP ViT-L/14 have low clarity. Clarity correlates 0.75 with top-sample activation, and firing rate also correlates positively with clarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretability of SAE latents in CLIP rises with their activation strength.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE space yields far more unique concept labels than PCA, and larger CLIP models yield more concepts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE bases recover more diverse concepts than neural or PCA bases, increasing with model size.

record.problems: The study focuses on final-block class-token embeddings and SAE components rather than individual neurons or earlier-layer dynamics. The authors also note that semantic alignment depends on CLIP-Mobile-S2, which may itself have spurious correlations or language ambiguity.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted. The paper's CLIP prompt-robustness and melanoma-classifier results were not included because they concern downstream semantic ambiguity and spurious-cue reliance, not neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: Individual neurons in vision models responding to unrelated inputs; neurons are not examined directly.
No language-model MLP neurons are studied.
No test of superposition as the cause; it is only cited as motivation.
No test of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
No comparison of polysemantic-neuron share across activation functions, architectures or regularization.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No test of how activation range or explanation scoring changes neuron polysemanticity judgments. The clarity-activation correlation concerns SAE latents only.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from discusses/T6 to assumes/T4. The paper takes neuron polysemanticity as its premise for using SAEs but never measures it. The 'polysemous' failure modes concern ambiguous words in text prompts (e.g. 'crane'), not polysemantic neurons, and should not be linked to any version.

versions.untested_parts: Whether individual neurons in image classifiers respond to several unrelated inputs.
Language-model MLP neurons and their responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether superposition or capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity.
Whether initialization, regularization, or training noise causes polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Whether architecture, activation function, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons or its performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related jobs when examined with better tools.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-L/14
rows.operation_detail: Measured clarity of SAE components and its correlation with activation on highly activating samples.

conditions.value: 17,455, filtered to those with ≥ 20 non-zero activations

rows.value: correlation 0.75; the majority of components exhibit low clarity
rows.note: This measures SAE-component clarity, not whether an individual neuron responds to several unrelated inputs.
rows.check: This is SAE-component clarity versus activation (r=0.75), not neuron polysemanticity. 'Low clarity' is measured on SAE latents, not neurons, so it cannot stand in for V1 or V7.

rows.subject: CLIP models; specific model variants not stated for this aggregate
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of unique concepts identified in SAE feature space with other representation bases.

conditions.value: inherent neural basis and PCA-transformed embeddings

rows.note: The aggregate concerns concept diversity, not the number or semantic coherence of individual neurons.
rows.check: It counts unique concept labels in SAE space (5,363) against PCA (<500). The neural-basis count appears only in Fig. 4b, with no number in the text. The comparison also includes the study's own preferred basis against alternatives, so it is not a measure of neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-H/14 and CLIP ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the number of unique concepts captured across model variants.
rows.value: ViT-H/14 showed over 20% more unique concepts
rows.note: This reports concept-set diversity, not polysemanticity of neurons.
rows.check: It reports concept diversity by model size (ViT-H/14 has over 20% more concepts than ViT-B/16). This is unrelated to the share of polysemantic neurons.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
